Fifty-four African countries have rejected any attempt to renegotiate the Paris Agreement, warning that reopening the global climate pact, particularly its obligations, would undermine commitments already agreed by countries to address climate change. The African Group of Negotiators on Climate Change said any attempt to alter the agreement was a red line for the continent, insisting that developed countries must honour their existing obligations rather than seek to revise the framework governing global climate action. The position comes as negotiations at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference, known as COP31, in Antalya, Türkiye, enter their final hours, with African countries pushing for stronger commitments on climate finance, adaptation and support for vulnerable economies. Speaking at a press conference on the state of negotiations on Thursday, the AGN Chair, Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, said Africa would not accept any attempt to renegotiate the Paris Agreement, particularly provisions relating to the responsibilities of countries. He said, “There’s one message that I also want to put across, which is about renegotiating the Paris Agreement. I think this is something that is a big red line for the African continent. We need to stay within the confines of the agreement because that is what we all have agreed in the past to do business with.” The chair’s remarks reflect growing concerns among developing countries that efforts to revisit existing climate commitments could weaken the obligations of developed nations to provide financial and other forms of support to countries bearing the brunt of climate change despite contributing relatively little to global greenhouse gas emissions. The dispute over climate finance has become one of the major sticking points at COP31, following changes to the proposed adaptation finance target in the latest draft decision released on November 19. Africa faults nations preaching fossil phase-out, pursuing oil deals BOI earmarks 10% of funding for green projects Group urges countries to match climate commitments with actions The revised draft dropped an earlier proposal requiring adaptation finance for developing countries to reach at least $120bn annually by 2035. The figure had been based on tripling the $40bn annual adaptation finance commitment under the Glasgow Climate Pact, agreed at COP26 in 2021. Under that commitment, developed countries agreed to double adaptation finance from approximately $20bn provided in 2019 to $40bn annually by 2025. However, the latest draft no longer specifies the $120bn figure or identifies the $40bn Glasgow commitment as the baseline for calculating the proposed increase. Instead, paragraph 40 retains a commitment to at least triple adaptation finance by 2035, while paragraph 43 requests the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change Standing Committee on Finance to prepare a technical report identifying possible baselines. Paragraph 44 also proposes developing an implementation pathway for the target. The removal of the specific financial figure raises concerns about how the proposed increase will be measured, funded and implemented, particularly as developing countries seek assurances that climate finance commitments will translate into actual resources. African countries have repeatedly argued that such financing should be predictable, accessible and largely provided through grants or highly concessional instruments rather than commercial loans that could deepen their debt burdens. Addressing questions about the continent’s ability to implement its climate commitments amid limited financing, Amoah said Africa’s concerns were not simply about securing additional money but ensuring that the financial architecture delivered resources on affordable terms.
